n: The gloom will not last. The northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali around Galilee, the first conquered by Assyria (732 BC), will later be honored. 2 Nephi 19:1 reads “by the way of the Red Sea.”

f.g: “Circle of the Gentiles” — a region with many non-Israelites.

f.w: by the way of the sea

n: People walking in darkness see a great light. Matthew tells us this was fulfilled when Jesus began His ministry in Galilee.

f.w: The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light

n: God has made the nation grow and filled it with joy like harvest festivals or soldiers dividing the spoils of victory. KJV reads “not increased the joy,” but 2 Nephi 19:3 reads “and increased the joy,” which fits the context and an alternate Hebrew reading.

f.g: The Hebrew lo can mean “not” or (spelled differently) “to it”; many modern translations agree with the Book of Mormon.

n: God has broken the yoke and rod of the oppressor, just as He did when Gideon’s small band defeated Midian. The Book of Mormon version omits “as in the day of Midian.”

f.g: A wooden bar on the neck of a work animal — a symbol of slavery.

n: Every soldier’s boot and blood-soaked garment will be burned as fuel. War itself will end.

f.g: Better “the boot of the tramping warrior.”

n: The heart of the chapter: a child will be born who will rule, with names describing His divine nature. Christians, including Latter-day Saints, see this fulfilled in Jesus Christ.

f.w: unto us a child is born

f.g: Possibly one title: “Wonderful Counselor” — a planner of marvels.

n: His rule and peace will keep growing without end. He will reign on David’s throne with justice forever, and the Lord’s zeal will make it happen.
Isaiah returns to the present: the Lord has sent a message of judgment against Jacob, and it has landed on Israel — the northern kingdom.

f.g: Here the northern kingdom of Israel.

n: All Ephraim and Samaria will learn, even though they speak in proud defiance.
They boast: “The bricks fell? We’ll rebuild with stone. The cheap sycamores were cut down? We’ll replace them with cedar.” They refuse to see disaster as a call to repent.

f.g: Common fig-mulberry trees, used for cheap lumber.

n: So the Lord will raise up Rezin’s enemies against Israel and stir up its foes.
Syria from the east and the Philistines from the west will devour Israel. Yet God’s anger isn’t finished, and His hand remains stretched out — a refrain repeated four times.

f.w: his hand is stretched out still

n: Despite being struck, the people still don’t turn back to the God who disciplines them.
So the Lord will cut off Israel’s leaders and followers alike in a single day — head and tail, palm branch and reed.

f.g: Palm branch and reed — the high and the low.

n: The “head” is the elders and nobles; the “tail” is the false prophets who teach lies.
The leaders mislead the people, and those who follow them are ruined.
So wicked has the nation become that even its young men, orphans, and widows — usually objects of God’s special mercy — are caught up in hypocrisy and foolish speech. Still His hand is stretched out.
Wickedness itself spreads like a wildfire through brush and forest, rising in clouds of smoke. Sin destroys from within.
Under God’s judgment the land is scorched, the people become fuel for the fire, and no one spares even his brother.
In a famine of the soul and body, people grab on every side but are never satisfied, and turn on one another — even their own kin.

f.w: the flesh of his own arm
f.g: Perhaps “his neighbor” — they devour their own people.

n: Brother tribes Manasseh and Ephraim fight each other, then unite only to attack Judah. Civil war tore Israel apart in its final years. Still His hand is stretched out.

f.g: The two tribes descended from Joseph’s sons (Genesis 48).
